entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jonas of Orléans (d. 843 CE) emerged as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in the Carolingian Empire, serving as Bishop of Orléans from 818 until his death. His career unfolded during the tumultuous reign of Emperor Louis the Pious, a period marked by intense internal conflicts over imperial succession and the consolidation of Christian moral authority across Francia. Jonas was not merely an administrator; he was a leading intellectual and a key architect of Carolingian reform, deeply involved in shaping the moral and legal framework of the Frankish Church and state, particularly through his influential writings on kingship, ecclesiastical discipline, and the duties of Christian rulers. His contributions significantly influenced the relationship between secular and spiritual power in the post-Charlemagne era.

Appointed to the important see of Orléans, Jonas quickly rose to prominence, becoming a trusted advisor to Louis the Pious. He played a crucial role in the synods of the early 9th century, notably the Council of Paris in 825 and the Council of Thionville in 835, where he helped formulate decrees on clerical conduct, monastic reform, and the proper governance of the empire according to Christian principles. His most celebrated works include *De institutione regia* (c. 831), a mirror for princes dedicated to Pippin I of Aquitaine, which articulated a rigorous vision of kingship based on justice and piety, and *De cultu imaginum*, a defense of the Western position against Byzantine iconoclasm. He also participated actively in the political machinations surrounding the succession crisis of the 830s, often siding with the emperor against his rebellious sons, though his primary aim remained the moral order of the realm.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jonas of Orléans significantly shaped Carolingian political theology through his influential writings like *De institutione regia*, which defined Christian kingship for centuries. His role in major synods also directly contributed to the standardization of ecclesiastical law and monastic reform across the Frankish realm.
